newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria bank battle exposes coalition fracture.
newsitem.headline: Austria bank battle exposes coalition fracture.

text.p: Austria's two-party government clung to life on Sunday after striking a deal over a major bank privatisation, but the battle exposed serious fault lines in a coalition that has ruled for nearly 11 years.

Social Democrat Chancellor Franz Vranitzky and Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel, leader of the conservative People's Party, finally agreed to sell the country's most prestigious bank, Creditanstalt-Bankverein, ending weeks of bitter recrimination and poisoned relations.

After 11 hours of crisis talks on Saturday, the conservatives lost the main fight -- to stop Creditanstalt, long considered its fiefdom, from being sold to Bank Austria, the bank that likes to say "Yes" to the Social Democrats.

"The People's Party last night suffered a major political defeat for putting the interests of its party before the economic interests of the country," Green Party leader Christoph Chorherr said in a statement.
"The coalition crisis was not solved, it has merely been postponed," he added.

While Schuessel won significant concessions from the Social Democrats, including the eventual privatisation of Bank Austria, Vranitzky's party will be main player in the banking industry for years to come.

"This is a compromise with strong advantages for the Social Democrats because the influence of the party has been secured for many years," Josef Ertl, chief political editor of the respected Standard newspaper, told Reuters.
Vranitzky was buoyant on announcing the sale in the early hours of Sunday morning, telling reporters they had written off the government far too soon.
"As I said before the talks, there was no need to prepare a funeral dirge or compose a requiem (for the government)," he said. "We have shown...that the government is a unified body."
Far right leader Joerg Haider, happy to make capital out of a government split, said on Sunday the conservatives showed once again they just could not win when the chips were down.
Haider's nationalist Freedom Party came within a few thousand votes of the two main parties in European elections last October, scoring nearly 28 percent of the vote.

The anti-immigration, Euro-sceptic party has already won over a sizeable chunk of Vranitzky's working class support and hopes to persuade conservatives they can only retain real power by joining him in a coalition government in the future.
Liberal Forum party leader Heide Schmidt lambasted the coalition for subjecting the Austrian people to what she called "a frightening spectacle" over the past few weeks.
The two parties were unable to stop playing politics with the economy, she said.
The political repercussions for the conservatives were still unclear, with Bank Austria likely to start cutting the workforce of the merged banks of around 16,000 employees.

Creditanstalt's workers, many of them conservative supporters who had opposed the Bank Austria bid, fear they will now come under the axe. Through a quirk in employment law, Creditanstalt employees are easier to sack than Bank Austria's.
One thing was clear -- the carve-up of the economy and major institutions between the two megaliths of Austria's post-1945 politics was breaking down.
